newsitem.title: UK: London gold fixes easier as dollar turns firmer.
newsitem.headline: London gold fixes easier as dollar turns firmer.

text.p: Gold prices eased back on Thursday afternoon as the dollar strengthened against European currencies in the wake of Germany's row over gold reserve revaluation.

Dealers said the market's reaction remained muted to news late on Wednesday that the Bundesbank had rejected Bonn's proposal to revalue its gold reserves and use the paper profit to help the country meet European Monetary Union entry rules.
"Movements in the PGMs (platinum group metals) are more significant for gold than what's up in Bonn," one dealer said.
Gold was fixed at $343.90 per ounce down from $345.70 this morning and compared to $342.80 on Wednesday afternoon.
The June Comex contract was down $0.30 at $345.00.

The dollar edged above 1.70 marks as German politicians and economic commentators exchanged opinions on the desirability or otherwise of up-valuing the country's 95 million ounces of gold reserves closer to their market value.

Analysts had mixed views on the outcome of the Bonn-Bundesbank disagreement and also on fudging start-up criteria to get European Monetary Union (EMU) in place on schedule in 1999. How this would affect gold was also debatable.
"If the Bundesbank wins this and there seems to be a chance that it will, it will keep the debate going on gold reserves and that will not be good for the market," one analyst said.
Another view was that it was a net positive for gold as investors may prefer to seek out gold as a safe haven while the argument raged.
Palladium tried to better Wednesday's stab at $200 but could not sustain it. After some selling on Nymex it was indicated at $182.00/$188.00 down about $14 from Wednesday's close.
Platinum in contrast was about $8.00 firmer at $409.50/$415.50 in a trading range of $401.00-$425.00.
Dealers said the one-month borrowing rate in both metals was steepening daily and was indicated at 33 percent for platinum and 50 percent for palladium.
"If you have to borrow you have to pay and accept the pain," one dealer said, adding that the alternative was taking a price risk in markets with a swingeing daily range of around $20.00.
The start up of Russia's delayed 1997 export campaign, the main cause of scarcity of supply, was due this week or next Russian officials said last week.
"There's no sign of deliveries yet as far as we can see," one dealer said.
Silver was quiet and marked up five cents to $4.76/$4.78.
